text: Welcome to the Intermediate Capstone. This course picks up right where the Beginner project left off, with the same retail chain, the same medallion pipeline, and two new problems that showed up at the same time. Over this chapter you're going to redesign that pipeline to be incremental, using Delta Lake's real merge-into capability, and add a brand new Gold table along the way.

Quick recap of where things stand. The Beginner project built one pipeline to answer one question for Store Operations: how did we do yesterday. That became gold-dot-daily-sales-summary, one row per store per day, holding total sales and total transactions. The pipeline that builds it runs a full reload every night — it reprocesses everything from scratch. At the data volumes that project worked with, that was simple, correct, and fast enough.

Now a Regional Manager — someone who oversees multiple stores, not just one — has a new question. They don't just want total sales per store per day. They want to see which categories are driving that number, and whether that differs store to store. The existing Gold table was deliberately built without a category dimension at all, so it simply can't answer this. That's not a bug. It's a brand new requirement.

At the same time, a completely separate problem has been building quietly in the background. Bronze-dot-sales-raw has been accumulating every day since the Beginner project went live, and the nightly job still reprocesses all of that accumulated history, every single night, just to pick up one new day's worth of transactions. The numbers are still correct — this isn't a correctness bug. It's a scale problem: runtime keeps growing with total history, and the overnight batch window isn't getting any longer.

It would be easy to lump these together, but they genuinely have different causes. One is a brand new business requirement; the other is an existing pipeline running out of room to scale. What ties them together is that they share one solution. Once Bronze and Silver move from reprocessing everything to processing only what's new, adding a second Gold table for the Regional Manager becomes straightforward, and the nightly runtime stops growing with history.

So that's the chapter ahead: two real problems, one incremental redesign, and a second Gold table — gold-dot-category-breakdown — built on top of it. Next lesson, before touching any new code, you'll plan exactly how Bronze, Silver, and Gold each change shape to make all of this possible.
